identification.summary: Aoqin Dragon is a China-linked cyberespionage cluster that SentinelLabs disclosed in June 2022. SentinelLabs says it has been active since at least 2013 and mainly targets organizations in Southeast Asia and Australia [S1][S5]. Its main focus is espionage against targets in Australia, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Singapore and Vietnam [S1]. Targeted sectors are government, education and telecommunications [S3][S7]. The group uses document lures, some on regional political affairs and some pornographic, and relies heavily on USB shortcut techniques and fake removable devices. Intrusions usually drop one of two backdoors: Mongall or a modified version of the open-source Heyoka project [S1][S3][S7].
identification.firstObserved: SentinelLabs: active since at least 2013 [S1]. Coverage of the report describes exploit-document campaigns running from 2012 to 2015 [S8][S9].
identification.notes: There is no Microsoft name for this cluster in the sources gathered. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as Aoqin Dragon (G1007) [S2]. SentinelLabs assesses with moderate confidence a possible link to the cluster Mandiant tracks as UNC94 [S1][S4], and reports some tactical association with Naikon [S8]. These are possible overlaps, not merges.

attribution.sponsor: No government or vendor source gathered names a sponsoring state organization. SentinelLabs describes the actor as a small Chinese-speaking team whose targeting closely aligns with the Chinese government's political interests [S1][S7].
attribution.confidence: SentinelLabs assesses with moderate confidence that Aoqin Dragon is a small Chinese-speaking team with possible ties to Naikon and UNC94 [S1][S4][S8]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: The assessment rests on SentinelLabs' malware, infrastructure and victimology analysis [S1], on Chinese-government-aligned targeting [S7], and on tooling and tactical overlaps with UNC94 and Naikon [S4][S8]. Vietnam's Authority of Information Security (AIS/NCSC) named Aoqin Dragon among APT groups expanding command-and-control infrastructure in the first half of 2022, but did not attribute it to a state [S6].

objectives: Long-term espionage against government, education and telecommunications organizations in the Asia-Pacific region [S1][S3]. SentinelLabs says the targeting closely aligns with Chinese government political interests [S7]. Decoy content mostly targets readers interested in APAC political affairs [S7].

targeting.notes: Country list per SentinelLabs [S1]. Vietnam's AIS/NCSC told agencies to monitor for and block connections to listed Aoqin Dragon infrastructure in mid-2022 [S6].

capabilities.summary: Initial access, per SentinelLabs reporting: (1) weaponized documents exploiting the old, already-patched Office flaws CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2010-3333, mainly in 2012-2015 [S8][S9]; (2) fake antivirus executables; and (3) forged removable-device folders, used since at least 2018, that trick users into opening the wrong folder and running the malware [S4][S7][S9]. The malware copies itself to real removable devices attached to the host, which spreads it through USB shortcut techniques [S3][S10]. For defense evasion it uses DLL hijacking, Themida-packed files and DNS tunneling [S8][S2]. Mongall, in use since about 2013, is a simple implant that provides a remote shell and file upload and download [S9]. The modified Heyoka is more capable: it can kill processes, manipulate files and collect process information [S9]. The original Heyoka project exfiltrates data over spoofed DNS requests, and the actor loads its version through DLL injection [S3].

campaigns.name: Exploit-document phase
campaigns.summary: Weaponized documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158 and CVE-2010-3333 deliver backdoors. Lures are themed on APAC political affairs or are pornographic.

campaigns.name: Mongall backdoor in use
campaigns.summary: SentinelLabs dates Aoqin Dragon activity and the Mongall implant to at least 2013.

campaigns.name: Fake removable device phase
campaigns.summary: From 2018 the actor adds fake removable devices and fake antivirus lures alongside document exploits, and spreads through USB shortcuts.

campaigns.name: SentinelLabs public disclosure
campaigns.summary: SentinelLabs publishes the Aoqin Dragon report, covering about ten years of espionage against Southeast Asia and Australia and a moderate-confidence possible link to UNC94.

campaigns.name: Vietnam AIS dispatch 941/CATTT-NCSC
campaigns.summary: Vietnam's Authority of Information Security says several APT groups, including Aoqin Dragon, expanded C2 infrastructure in the first half of 2022. It orders agencies to monitor for and block the listed IPs and domains.

diamond.adversary: SentinelLabs assesses with moderate confidence a small Chinese-speaking team with possible ties to UNC94 and Naikon [S1][S8].
diamond.capability: Exploit documents (CVE-2012-0158, CVE-2010-3333), fake antivirus lures, fake removable devices and USB propagation, DLL hijacking, Themida packing, and the Mongall and modified Heyoka backdoors with DNS-based C2 and exfiltration [S3][S8][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled C2 IPs and domains. Vietnam's AIS reported this infrastructure expanding in the first half of 2022 and published blocking indicators [S6]. DNS tunneling is used for C2 and exfiltration [S3][S8].
diamond.victim: Government, education and telecommunications organizations in Australia, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Singapore and Vietnam [S1][S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection aligned with Chinese government political interests in the Asia-Pacific region, including regional political affairs [S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints running unpatched Microsoft Office, plus environments where removable media is shared, which the USB propagation exploits [S3][S8][S10].

gaps: The SentinelLabs primary report, MITRE G1007 page, Avertium and Security Affairs pages could not be fetched directly (DNS resolution blocked). Their content is taken from search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
The khonggianmang.vn PDF (CB_941) in the imported record was not opened. The dispatch is cited through a provincial republication, and its IOC appendix was not reviewed.
No public reporting on Aoqin Dragon activity after mid-2022 was found. Current operational status is unknown.

The UNC94 and Naikon links are only SentinelLabs assessments (moderate confidence or 'possible'). Mandiant's own UNC94 reporting was not located. Microsoft and other vendor naming for the cluster is unknown.
The start date is inconsistent across sources: 'at least 2013' in SentinelLabs versus exploit campaigns dated 2012-2015 in secondary coverage.
Specific victim organizations, dwell times and data stolen are not public in the sources gathered.
No government (US, Australian or other Five Eyes) attribution or advisory naming Aoqin Dragon was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key terrain is government, education and telecom networks in Australia and Southeast Asia, including partner-nation networks that coalition operations depend on. Removable-media transfer paths across air gaps or between enclaves are a relevant avenue [S1][S3]. STEP 2 (effects): The actor's reliance on old Office exploits and USB propagation means poorly patched systems and ones with weak media control are the most exposed. DNS tunneling can carry C2 through networks that only lightly inspect DNS [S3][S8][S9]. STEP 3 (adversary model): The template is a political or pornographic decoy document, fake antivirus or fake removable-device folder, followed by DLL-hijacked or Themida-packed Mongall or Heyoka, DNS-based C2, and spread to attached USB devices [S7][S8][S9][S10]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is quiet, long-duration espionage against regional government and telecom targets aligned with PRC political interests [S1][S7]. MDCOA is USB-borne spread into partner or coalition mission networks that share removable media with targeted regional agencies, enabling persistent collection on combined planning; this is an extrapolation, not reported activity. Candidate indicators: Office processes exploiting CVE-2012-0158 or CVE-2010-3333; executables masquerading as antivirus tools or as removable-drive folders; DLL side-loading from removable media; Themida-packed binaries; anomalous high-volume or encoded DNS queries; and hits on the Vietnamese AIS IOC list [S2][S6][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: fuse the Vietnamese AIS IOC list and SentinelLabs indicators into DNS and endpoint monitoring for Indo-Pacific mission partner networks [S1][S6]. Authorities: activity is espionage against foreign partner-nation and civilian networks. Response on partner networks depends on partner consent and information-sharing agreements, and any action beyond DoDIN defense needs separate authorities. Mission assurance: enforce removable-media controls, patch legacy Office and inspect DNS for tunneling on systems exchanging data with regional partners, because the actor relies on USB propagation and DNS C2 [S3][S8][S10]. Coordination: share detections with partner CERTs (for example Vietnam's AIS/NCSC, which already tracks the cluster [S6]) and with vendor reporting on the UNC94 and Naikon overlaps, keeping vendor confidence levels distinct from government attribution [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: SentinelLabs has uncovered a cluster of activity beginning at least as far back as 2013 and continuing to the present day, primarily targeting organizations in Southeast Asia and Australia. They assess that the threat actor's primary focus is espionage and relates to targets in Australia, Cambodia, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Vietnam. We track this activity as 'Aoqin Dragon'. The threat actor has a history of using document lures with pornographic themes to infect users and makes heavy use of USB shortcut techniques to spread the malware and infect additional targets. Attacks attributable to Aoqin Dragon typically drop one of two backdoors, Mongall and a modified version of the open source Heyoka project.
